{
  "passage_id": "AUSTEN_EMMA_002",
  "condition": "paraphrase",
  "rewritten_text": "The list she compiled when she was only fourteen—I recall thinking it gave her judgment great credit, so I kept it for a while; and I imagine she could now produce a very fine list. Yet I have given up hoping for any steady reading habit from Emma. She will never endure anything that demands industry and patience, nor will she bend her fancy to her understanding. Where Miss Taylor failed to inspire, I can safely say Harriet Smith will accomplish nothing. —You could never persuade her to read as much as you wished.—You know you could not.

“I suppose,” answered Mrs. Weston, smiling, “that I thought so then; but since we have been apart, I cannot recall Emma ever neglecting anything I asked of her.”

“There is scarcely any desire to revive such a memory,” said Mr. Knightley, feelingly; and for a moment or two he seemed to have done so. “But I,” he added promptly, “who have not been enchanted in that way, must still see, hear, and remember. Emma is spoiled by being the cleverest of her family. At ten she had the misfortune of being able to answer questions that baffled her sister at seventeen. She was always quick and confident; Isabella was slow and shy. And ever since she was twelve, Emma has been mistress of the house and of you all. In her mother she lost the only person capable of coping with her. She inherits her mother’s talents, and must have been under her influence.”

“I should have been sorry, Mr. Knightley, to rely on your recommendation, had I left Mr. Woodhouse’s family and sought another situation; I do not think you would have spoken a kind word for me to anyone. I am sure you always regarded me as unsuitable for the position I held.”

“Yes,” he said, smiling. “You are better placed here; very fit for a wife, but not at all for a governess. Yet you have been preparing yourself to be an excellent wife all the time you were at Hartfield. You might not give Emma such a complete education as your abilities would seem to promise; but you were receiving a very good education from her, especially on the matrimonial point of submitting your own will and doing as you were bid; and if Weston had asked me to recommend a wife for him, I should certainly have named Miss Taylor.”

“Thank you. There will be little merit in making a good wife for a man like Mr. Weston.”

“Honestly, I fear you are rather wasted, and that with every disposition to bear, there will be nothing to bear. We shall not despair, however. Weston may become irritable from indulgent comfort, or his son may trouble him.”

“I hope not that. It is unlikely. No, Mr. Knightley, do not predict vexation from that quarter.”

“Not I, indeed. I only mention possibilities. I do not claim Emma’s genius for foretelling and guessing. I hope, with all my heart, that the young man may be a Weston in merit and a Churchill in fortune. —But Harriet Smith—I have not half done about Harriet Smith. I think her the very worst sort of companion that Emma could possibly have."
}

“Mr. Elton’s manners are not perfect,” replied Emma, “but where there is a desire to please, one ought to overlook, and one does overlook a great deal. When a man does his best with only moderate powers, he will have the advantage over negligent superiority. Mr. Elton’s prospects, however, began to recover little by little. Though she did not experience the first spark of understanding as sharply as she might have done the day before, or even an hour earlier, her interest soon grew; and before their initial conversation ended, she had convinced herself of all the feelings of curiosity, astonishment, regret, pain and pleasure that this fortunate Miss Hawkins could inspire, feelings that would allow her to place the Martins in a proper subordinate position in her imagination.

Emma found herself rather pleased that such a meeting had taken place. It had served to blunt the initial shock without leaving any lingering alarm. As Harriet now lived, the Martins could not reach her without seeking her out, whereas before they had lacked either the courage or the condescension to do so; since she had refused the brother, the sisters had not visited Mrs. Goddard’s, and a whole year might pass without any necessity or even any opportunity for them to be thrown together again.

CHAPTER IV

Human nature is so inclined to favor those who find themselves in interesting circumstances that a young person who either marries or dies is sure to be spoken of kindly.

Not a week had passed since Miss Hawkins’s name first entered Highbury’s conversation before she was, by one means or another, discovered to possess every commendable quality of person and mind: handsome, elegant, highly accomplished, and perfectly amiable. When Mr. Elton himself arrived to celebrate his happy prospects and spread the news of her virtues, there was little left for him to do but mention her Christian name and state whose music she chiefly performed.

Mr. Elton returned a very contented man. He had gone away rejected and mortified—his sanguine hopes dashed after a series of what he had taken as strong encouragements; not only had he lost the right lady, but he found himself reduced to the level of a very unsuitable one. He had left deeply offended, yet he came back engaged to another—indeed, to a woman superior to the first, for in such circumstances what is gained always outweighs what is lost. He returned cheerful and self‑satisfied, eager and busy, caring nothing for Miss Woodhouse and defying Miss Smith.

The charming Augusta Hawkins, besides all the usual advantages of perfect beauty and merit, possessed an independent fortune of several thousand pounds—a sum that would always be spoken of as ten thousand, a point of both dignity and convenience. The story was told well; he had not thrown himself away—he had secured a woman of about ten thousand pounds, and he had done so with delightful rapidity. The first hour of their introduction was swiftly followed by distinguished notice; the account he gave Mrs. Cole of the rise and progress of the affair was glorious—the steps so quick, from the accidental encounter to the dinner at Mr. Green’s, and the party at Mrs. Brown’s—smiles and blushes increasing in importance, with consciousness and agitation richly scattered. The lady had been so easily impressed, so sweetly disposed, that, to use a most intelligible phrase, she was very ready to accept him, satisfying both vanity and prudence."
}

To my amazement, when he finally found me there, I realized I had been sitting with them for almost forty‑five minutes. The lady didn’t give me any chance to escape.

Her skin had a softness and delicacy that gave her face a special elegance.” He listened politely, admitted he had heard the same from others, but confessed that nothing could replace a healthy glow. A good complexion adds beauty to ordinary features, and when features are already fine, the effect is even better—though he need not try to describe it.

Growing more frightened, she immediately promised them money, took out her purse, handed over a shilling, and begged them not to demand more or to use her ill. She managed to walk away, though very slowly, but her terror and the sight of her purse proved too tempting; the whole gang closed in, demanding further payment.

At that moment Frank Churchill happened upon her, trembling and disordered, while the children were loud and insolent. By a most fortunate turn his departure from Highbury had been delayed, bringing him to her aid at this critical instant. The pleasant morning had prompted him to walk ahead, leaving his horses to meet him on another road a mile or two beyond Highbury. Having borrowed a pair of scissors from Miss Bates the night before and forgetting to return them, he stopped at her door for a few minutes, which made him later than intended; walking on foot, he remained unseen by the whole party until he was almost upon them. The terror the woman and boy had been inflicting on Harriet was now theirs to endure. He left them wholly frightened, and Harriet, clinging to him and scarcely able to speak, mustered enough strength to reach Hartfield before her spirits were completely overcome. I am a talker, you know; I am rather a talker; and now and then I have let a thing escape that I should not. I am not like Jane; I wish I were. I will answer for it—she never betrayed the slightest thing in the world. Where is she?—Oh! just behind. Perfectly remember Mrs. Perry’s coming.—Extraordinary dream, indeed!"

They were entering the hall. Mr. Knightley’s eyes had already glanced at Jane before Miss Bates’s did. From Frank Churchill’s face, where he seemed to hide or laugh away confusion, his gaze involuntarily fell on hers; but she was indeed just behind, busy with her shawl. Mr. Weston entered, and the two other gentlemen waited at the door to let her pass. Mr. Knightley thought Frank Churchill was determined to catch her eye—he seemed watching her intently—but in vain, for Jane passed between them into the hall without looking at either of them.

There was no time for further comment or explanation. The dream had to be endured, and Mr. Knightley took his seat with the others around the large modern circular table that Emma had introduced at Hartfield, a piece only she could have persuaded her father to place there instead of the small Pembroke table on which he had taken his two daily meals for forty years. Tea was served pleasantly, and no one seemed in a hurry to leave.

"Miss Woodhouse," said Frank Churchill after reaching for a table behind him, "have your nephews taken away their alphabet blocks—their box of letters? It used to sit here. Where is it? This is a rather dull‑looking evening, more suited to winter than summer. We had great fun with those letters one morning. I want to puzzle you again."

Emma liked the idea, and when the box was produced the table was quickly covered with the alphabet blocks, which no one seemed more eager to use than the two of them. They swiftly formed words for each other, or for anyone else who might be puzzled. The quiet nature of the game made it especially suitable for Mr. Woodhouse, who had often been distressed by the more lively diversions Mr. Weston sometimes introduced, and who now sat happily occupied, lamenting with tender melancholy the departure of the "poor little boys," and fondly pointing out, as he picked up any stray letter, how beautifully Emma had written it."
}

“Have you heard from her yourself this morning?” he exclaimed. “You have, I think, and you know the whole story.”

“No, I have not; I know nothing; please tell me.”

“You are prepared for the worst, I see—and it is indeed very bad. Harriet Smith is to marry Robert Martin.”

Emma started, clearly not prepared for such news, and her eyes, wide with eager surprise, seemed to say, “No, this cannot be!” though her lips remained shut.

“It is true,” continued Mr. Knightley, “I have it straight from Robert Martin himself. He left me not even half an hour ago.”

She continued to stare at him, her amazement almost speaking for her.

“You like it, my Emma, as little as I feared. I wish we could agree on this, but in time we may. Time, you may be sure, will make one of us think differently; meanwhile we need not discuss the matter at length.”

“You misunderstand me, you completely misunderstand me,” she replied, forcing herself. “It is not that such a circumstance would make me unhappy now, but I cannot believe it. It seems impossible!—You cannot be saying that Harriet Smith has accepted Robert Martin. You cannot be saying he has even proposed to her yet—only that he intends it.”

“I mean that he has done it,” answered Mr. Knightley, smiling yet resolute, “and she has accepted.”

“Good God!” she cried. “Well!”—and, using her workbasket as an excuse to lower her face and hide the intense delight and amusement she felt, she added, “Now tell me everything; make it clear to me. How, where, when?—Let me know it all. I have never been more surprised—but it does not make me unhappy, I assure you. How—how was it possible?”

“It is a very simple story. He went to town on business three days ago, and I persuaded him to take charge of some papers I needed to send to John. He delivered those papers to John’s chambers, and John invited him to join their party that evening at Astley’s. They were taking the two eldest boys to Astley’s—our brother and sister, Henry, John, and Miss Smith. My friend Robert could not resist. They called for him on the way; everyone was extremely amused; and my brother asked him to dine with them the next day—which he did. During that visit, as I understand it, he found a chance to speak with Harriet, and he certainly did not speak in vain. She accepted, making him as happy as he deserves. He returned yesterday by coach and was with me this morning right after breakfast, to report his actions, first concerning my affairs and then his own. That is all I can relate about the how, where, and when. Your friend Harriet will have a much longer story to tell when you see her."
}

They came from a respectable family in the north of England, a fact that impressed their memories more deeply than the knowledge that both their brother’s and their own fortunes had been derived from trade.

Mr. Bingley inherited property amounting to nearly a hundred thousand pounds from his father, who had intended to purchase an estate but died before doing so. Mr. Bingley had the same intention, and sometimes chose a county for his home; yet, now that he possessed a fine house and the freedom of a manor, many who knew his easy temperament doubted whether he would not spend the rest of his days at Netherfield and leave the next generation to acquire a new estate.

His sisters were eager that he should have an estate of his own; but although he was now only a tenant, Miss Bingley was by no means reluctant to preside at his table, and Mrs. Hurst, who had married a man of more fashion than fortune, was equally inclined to regard his house as her home whenever it suited her. Mr. Bingley had not yet reached his twenty‑second year when, by a chance recommendation, he was invited to view Netherfield House. He inspected it for half an hour, liked the situation and the principal rooms, was satisfied with the owner’s praise, and took it at once.

Mrs. Bennet, smiling and encouraging, warned him against the very Jane he had chosen. She said she could not speak for her younger daughters, but she felt it was her duty to hint that her eldest daughter would probably be engaged very soon.

Mr. Collins quickly switched his attention from Jane to Elizabeth, and did so while Mrs. Bennet was tending the fire. Elizabeth, who was almost as young and as pretty as Jane, naturally became his new choice.

Mrs. Bennet kept the hint in mind and hoped she might soon have two daughters married. The man she could not stand to talk about the day before was now in her good graces.

Lydia still wanted to walk to Meryton, and every sister except Mary agreed to go with her. Mr. Collins was asked to join them by Mr. Bennet, who was eager to get rid of him and have his library to himself. After breakfast, Collins followed Mr. Bennet to the library, where he pretended to read a large volume while actually chatting nonstop with Mr. Bennet about his house and garden at Hunsford. This annoyed Mr. Bennet a great deal. He liked his library to be a quiet place, and although he expected foolishness and vanity in the other rooms, he was used to peace there. So he promptly invited Mr. Collins to accompany his daughters on their walk. Collins, who was actually more suited to walking than reading, gladly closed his big book and went.

They walked in a pompous, self‑important manner, while the cousins politely agreed to go along. Their walk continued until they reached Meryton. By then the younger sisters were no longer interested in Mr. Collins. Their eyes immediately looked up the street for the officers, and only a very smart hat or a new piece of muslin in a shop window could catch their attention.

Soon, however, every lady’s gaze was drawn to a young man they had never seen before, who looked very gentlemanly and was walking with an officer on the opposite side of the road. The officer was Mr. Denny, the very man Lydia had asked about when he returned from London, and he bowed as they passed. Everyone was struck by the stranger’s appearance and wondered who he was. The fact remains that we are very different kinds of men, and he despises me.”

“That is most shocking! He ought to be publicly disgraced.”
“He may be disgraced someday—but not by me. Until I can forget his father, I cannot confront or expose him.”

“A deep, resolute dislike of me—a dislike I can only partly ascribe to jealousy. If the late Mr. Darcy had cared for me less, his son might have tolerated me better; but his father’s unusual attachment to me irritated him early on. He lacked the temperament to endure the rivalry in which we found ourselves—the preferential treatment I often received.”

“I had not imagined Mr. Darcy to be so vile—though I never liked him, I had not thought him so ill. I presumed he despised people in general, but I did not suspect him of such malicious revenge, such injustice, such inhumanity!”

His unexpected proposal startled her so much that, without really knowing what she was doing, she accepted. He withdrew at once, leaving her to brood over her own lack of presence of mind; Charlotte tried to comfort her.

“I dare say you will find him very agreeable.”

“Heaven forbid! That would be the greatest misfortune of all! To find a man agreeable whom one is determined to hate! Do not wish me such an evil.”

When the dancing resumed and Darcy came again to claim her hand, Charlotte could not help whispering a warning, urging her not to be a fool and let her fancy for Wickham make her appear disagreeable in the eyes of a man whose consequences are often severe. Elizabeth gave no answer and took her place in the set, astonished at the dignity of being allowed to stand opposite Mr. Darcy, and reading in the looks of those around her the same amazement. They stood for a while without a word; she imagined their silence would last through both dances and, at first, resolved not to break it. Then, thinking it might be a greater penalty to her partner to force him to speak, she offered a slight remark about the dance. He replied, then fell silent again. After a few minutes she addressed him a second time,

“It is your turn to say something now, Mr. Darcy. I have spoken about the dance, and you ought to comment on the size of the room or the number of couples.”

He smiled and assured her that whatever she wished him to say would be said.

“Very well; that answer will suffice for the present. Perhaps later I may observe that private balls are far more pleasant than public ones; but now we may remain silent.”

“Do you speak by rule while you are dancing?”

“Sometimes. One must converse a little, you know. It would look odd to be entirely silent for half an hour together; yet, for the benefit of some, conversation should be arranged so that they have the trouble of saying as little as possible.”

“Are you considering your own feelings in this case, or do you think you are satisfying mine?”

“Both,” replied Elizabeth sharply; “for I have always seen a great similarity in the turn of our minds. We are each of an unsocial, taciturn disposition, unwilling to speak unless we expect to say something that will astonish the whole room and be handed down to posterity with all the éclat of a proverb.”

“This is not a very striking likeness to your own character, I am sure,” said he. “How near it may be to mine, I cannot pretend to say. You think it a faithful portrait, undoubtedly.”

“I must not judge my own performance.”"
}

  "rewritten_text": "It was Mr. Collins’s description of Hunsford and Rosings that had become, at last, reasonably softened; and Elizabeth realized that she would have to wait for her own journey there before she could learn the rest.

Jane had already sent a short note to her sister, announcing their safe arrival in London; and when she wrote again, Elizabeth hoped she would be able to say something about the Bingleys.

Her eagerness for this second letter was rewarded, as impatience often is. Jane had spent a week in the city without either seeing or hearing from Caroline. She explained it by supposing that her last letter to her friend at Longbourn had somehow been lost.

“My aunt,” she continued, “is going tomorrow into that part of town, and I shall take the opportunity of calling in Grosvenor Street.”

She wrote again after the visit was made, and after she had seen Miss Bingley. “I did not think Caroline in spirits,” she wrote, “but she was very glad to see me, and reproached me for giving her no notice of my coming to London. I was right, therefore; my last letter had never reached her. I inquired after their brother, of course. He was well, but so much engaged with Mr. Darcy that they scarcely ever saw him. I found that Miss Darcy was expected to dinner: I wish I could see her. My visit was not long, as Caroline and Mrs. Hurst were going out. I dare say I shall soon see them here.”

Elizabeth shook her head over this letter. It convinced her that only an accident could have revealed to Mr. Bingley her sister’s presence in town.

Four weeks passed, and Jane saw nothing of him. She tried to convince herself that she did not regret it; but she could no longer ignore Miss Bingley’s indifference. After waiting at home each morning for a fortnight, and inventing a fresh excuse each evening for her, the visitor finally appeared; yet the brevity of her stay, and especially the change in her manner, left Jane unable to deceive herself any longer. The letter she wrote on that occasion to her sister shows what she felt:

“My dearest Lizzy, I am sure you will be unable to triumph in your better judgment at my expense when I confess that I have been completely misled by Miss Bingley’s regard for me. Yet, dear sister, although the event has proved you right, do not think me obstinate if I still maintain that, given her behaviour, my confidence was as natural as your suspicion. I do not at all understand her reason for wishing to be intimate with me; but, if the same circumstances were to happen again, I am sure I would be deceived again. Caroline did not return my visit until yesterday; and not a note, not a line, did I receive in the meantime. When she did come, it was evident that she took no pleasure in it; she offered a brief, formal apology for not calling earlier, said nothing about wishing to see me again, and was, in every respect, such a changed creature that when she left I was perfectly resolved to cease the acquaintance. I pity her, though I cannot help blaming her.”"
}
